q: Of the three grapes traditionally written into the Valpolicella blend, one is no longer compulsory. Which one?
exp: Molinara is pale and low in tannin, and many growers felt it thinned the wine, so it became optional. Corvina still has to lead, with Rondinella filling a defined minority share.

q: Reckoned from the first of January after the harvest, how long must an Amarone rest before it may be released?
exp: Two years for the standard wine on that January clock, while the Riserva runs four years from the first of November of the harvest year. Most estates hold it far longer than the rule asks, because the tannin drawn out of shrivelled fruit takes time to settle.

q: Soave Classico covers the hills of the walled town itself and those of one neighbouring commune. Name that commune.
exp: The Classico zone straddles a boundary between two geologies, calcareous ground on the Soave side and volcanic on the Monteforte side. Everything beyond those hills is plain Soave, much of it grown on the flat.

q: Dark rock laid down by undersea eruptions underlies Soave's finest hills and is credited for the wine's saline tension. Name that rock.
exp: The eruptions happened underwater in the Eocene, which is why the basalt sits interleaved with marine limestone. Growers separate the two: basalt sites give a tighter, smokier Garganega, limestone a softer and more floral one.

q: Veneto's first DOCG, granted in 1998, was not a dry wine at all but a sweet one from dried grapes. Name it.
exp: Garganega dries well because its skins are thick and its bunches loose, so air moves through them. Recioto della Valpolicella is the red equivalent and a different wine entirely, which is why the second half of the name is the part that matters.

q: Bunches for Amarone spend the winter in a purpose-built loft with through-draughts on every side. What is that room called in Italian?
exp: Airflow, not warmth, is what keeps rot off the fruit, so the lofts are built high and open with fans now doing what the wind used to. Bunches are laid in single layers on racks or in shallow crates so nothing touches.

q: On a Conegliano Valdobbiadene label one word introduces a single steep hillside belonging to a named village. Which word?
exp: There are forty-three of them, and a Rive wine must be hand-harvested and carry a vintage. The word is the local dialect for a steep slope rather than a legal quality tier.

q: A cloudy Prosecco refermented in bottle and left undisgorged on its lees carries which traditional name?
exp: Col fondo means with the bottom, and the sediment is meant to be there. It was the farmhouse style before tanks arrived, and it comes out drier, savoury and gently hazy.

q: Volcanic hills between Soave and Vicenza grow a white grape so high in acid that it is used almost only for sparkling wine. Which grape?
exp: Durella takes its name from the hardness of its skin and keeps searing acidity even when fully ripe. Long lees ageing is what makes the traditional-method wines approachable, though tank method still accounts for the larger share of production.

q: Within Valdobbiadene a single steep hill of about a hundred hectares is the most prized site of the whole denomination. Name it.
exp: The slope is so steep that everything is carried by hand, and it is traditionally finished slightly sweeter than the rest of the zone. Land there is among the most expensive vineyard in Italy.

q: At Breganze, bunches of Vespaiola are twisted onto wires and hung to shrivel for a sweet wine. Name that wine.
exp: Torcolato comes from torcere, to twist, which is exactly what is done to the bunches before they are hung. The grape keeps ferocious acidity, so the finished wine is sweet without being cloying.

q: South of Lake Garda a white blend shares its stretch of morainic hills with Bardolino. Name that denomination.
exp: The blend leans on Garganega with Trebbiano Toscano, Friulano and Cortese filling it out, so it drinks rounder than Soave from the same lead grape. The zone sits almost wholly inside the southern half of Bardolino, which runs a good deal further north up the lake, and many estates make both.

q: Volcanic cones rise straight out of the plain southwest of Padua and carry a DOCG for sweet Moscato Giallo. Name those hills.
exp: The wine is Fior d'Arancio, orange blossom, which is exactly what Moscato Giallo smells of. The hills are old volcanic intrusions that never erupted through the surface, so they stand isolated above flat farmland.

q: Layered marl and sandstone flysch underlies the Collio, and growers there have their own word for it. What is that word?
exp: Ponca weathers quickly into a shallow, poor, free-draining soil that vines root into readily. It is the same Eocene flysch that continues over the border into Slovenian Brda under the name opoka.

q: A Friulian sweet-wine grape sets only a fraction of the flowers it opens, so its yields are minute. Which grape?
exp: The condition is called floral abortion, and it leaves bunches with a scatter of berries and plenty of air between them. Those loose bunches dry beautifully, which is the one advantage of an otherwise ruinous defect.

q: Verduzzo Friulano dried for a golden sweet wine holds DOCG rank in the hills above Nimis. Name that wine.
exp: Verduzzo is unusual among sweet-wine grapes for its tannin, which comes off the skins and gives the wine grip against the sugar. The zone is tiny, steep and among the coldest vineyard land in the region.
